title: 善意透支：主机品牌的品牌价值与用户忠诚正面临考验
content:
Goodwill Hunting: Consoles’ brand value and loyalty is being tested | Opinion | GamesIndustry.biz

There’s a really important piece of context that looms behind every decision, every announcement, and every news story about PlayStation or Xbox at the moment. It’s a ticking clock; a countdown to the moment when Sony and Microsoft are going to have to start talking about their next-generation hardware – and begin the process of convincing the world that an almost certainly
astronomical price point
isn’t a deal-breaker.
That’s going to be a difficult task under any circumstances. Game consoles do offer genuinely good value in terms of the hours of entertainment they provide over their lifespans, but the market for them is price-sensitive nonetheless. If PS6 ends up coming in at twice the launch price tag of the PS5, or perhaps even more, it’s going to be a tough sell. Not an impossible sell – but both companies will need to use everything at their disposal to bring consumers on board at those kinds of prices.
Damage to a company’s public image makes it substantively harder to get people to spend their discretionary money on your products
One of the most powerful tools at their disposal is going to be customer goodwill. As nebulous as “goodwill” can sound at times, it’s an incredibly powerful force in a totally discretionary market like videogames. People’s buying choices are deeply influenced by their feelings about companies and brands. Damage to a company’s reputation or public image makes it materially, substantively harder to get people to spend their discretionary money on your products.
You’d think, then, that both PlayStation and Xbox would be on a charm offensive right now. Knowing just how much goodwill is going to be burned when they announce their next-gen price tags (or, alternatively,
reveal the deep compromises
they’ve had to make to keep those price tags in a sane range), both companies ought to be deeply focused on ensuring their reserves of that goodwill are topped off by any means available to them.
That context is important, I think, to understanding the odd little drama that played out this week over Hideo Kojima’s upcoming game, Physint. Originally announced at one of Sony’s State of Play events back in early 2024, the game was intended to be the next major collaboration between Kojima and Sony following Death Stranding. Sony’s Columbia Pictures division was also involved in some capacity. This week, however, Kojima Productions revealed that Sony had dropped the project, leaving the company seeking a new publisher for the game; Xbox Game Studios promptly
swooped in to pick up publishing rights
.
Sony's step back from Kojima Productions is understandable, but risky. |
Image credit:
Xbox
Taken in isolation, there are certainly two valid sides to this story. Death Stranding was generally very well received critically, but the franchise was not a particularly big commercial hit; sequel title Death Stranding 2: On The Beach reportedly sold around 2 million copies. Physint, meanwhile, was shaping up to be a massively expensive development project – Kojima hinted in an interview last year that the game was still five or six years out from launch. It’s not hard to see why Sony executives would weigh that likely budget in one hand and the commercial performance of Death Stranding in the other and decide to drop out – and reporting by Bloomberg today suggests that's
exactly what happened
.
It’s also, however, easy to see why Xbox would swoop on the title. Kojima’s name still carries enormous cachet, and Physint, as his return to the stealth-action genre of Metal Gear Solid, is a far surer commercial bet than the very experimental and downright weird Death Stranding ever was. Hollywood directors and actors talk about doing big blockbuster movies as a way to ‘pay their dues’ so that studios will fund their artistic passion projects – in this case, Sony appears to have betted big on Kojima’s arthouse project and then passed on his likely blockbuster. Even if their commercial calculation was valid, the optics of dropping an original IP from one of the most famous game developers in the world and letting their competitor pick it up aren’t great.
We’ll probably have to wait half a decade to see whether Sony or Microsoft made the better choice
Ordinarily, you could shrug and leave it at that. After all, we’ll probably have to wait half a decade to see whether Sony or Microsoft made the better choice in this situation. What we won’t have to wait half a decade for, though, is the aforementioned moment when these companies try to make the case for what will almost certainly be the most expensive consoles ever launched. One Kojima project won’t make or break the PS6, but dropping a previously announced high profile original game and having Xbox pick it up is a slowly seeping crack in the wall of that tank of goodwill they’re going to need to draw on so heavily for their next-gen launch.
It’s far from the only crack in that tank. Despite the very solid sales of the PS5 – which is approaching the 100 million mark, though price hikes are probably slowing its progress somewhat – Sony has had a pretty rough ride in some other respects in this generation, often in ways that have tarnished its brand and reputation with its customers to some degree.
Much of this is due to the ongoing fallout from the company’s ill-conceived pivot to live service development, which left it with big, embarrassing failures like Concord, a litany of negative stories about its seemingly dysfunctional multi-billion dollar acquisition, Bungie, and a weak first-party release slate due to resources being focused on live service games that mostly never saw the light of day.
